transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-06-29 16:00 UTC | Duration: 38m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ravi (Redwood SE), Jenna, Liam, Marco, Sara (joined 00:12)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for hopping on, um quick set expectations, 30 minutes for the round up then we'll do decisions and next steps.
[00:18] Jenna: yep sounds good, we want to focus on the TTFT numbers and the streaming hiccup from last week.
[00:25] Ravi: great. quick recap — last week we pushed the kernel hedging change and enabled prefix KV cache for short prompts, and we saw improvements on median TTFT but some microburst tail.
[00:40] Liam: to put numbers on it, baseline hosted model gave us median ~42ms, with hedging + cache we dropped to 28ms median for 16-token responses, but the 99.9th spiked to ~1.2s on certain microbursts.
[01:05] Marco: those spikes correlate with concurrent streaming handshakes, looks like the stream init path sometimes blocks on the kernel selection lock.
[01:20] Ravi: right, we suspected contention on the kernel selector when two different sequence-length lanes are created simultaneously — the runtime serializes some ops. we prototyped a non-blocking select; on our bench it's reduced the lock time by ~70%.
[01:40] Jenna: and that test was on your infra or ours?
[01:44] Ravi: internal bench, 16v100-equivalent; not exact to your c5-style nodes. need to validate on your staging.
[01:52] Maya: Sara, any high-level constraints for SLA / acceptable tail?
[01:56] Sara: we need 95% < 100ms for user-facing flows, ideally 99th < 250ms. long-term we'll push more load but pilot is about proving sub-100ms medians with predictable tails.
[02:17] Liam: also worth noting we have a seqlen distribution skew — 70% <= 32 tokens, 20% 33-128, 10% >128. so the fast path is vital.
[02:33] Ravi: good intel. that distribution means we should bias kernel choices to favor short-seq optimized kernels and prewarm KV caches.
[02:45] Jenna: on prewarm — how are you handling cold KV cache misses? we've seen first-token times balloon when a model variant switches.
[02:57] Ravi: two mitigations: 1) proactive prefix caching for the hot model variants during low traffic windows; 2) quick fallback to lower-precision quantized kernel that warms much faster. tradeoff is slight quality delta.
[03:18] Jenna: quality delta — do you have numbers?
[03:21] Ravi: for our sample, 8-bit quantized path changed perplexity by ~0.6% on the eval set; in human eval it's not statistically significant for short prompts. but for some safety-sensitive paths you may not accept any delta.
[03:38] Marco: we are also constrained by KMS policies — anything that moves keys out of our KMS boundary is non-starter. private deployment stuff we'll discuss later.
[03:49] Maya: right — okay, let's run through the issues list from last week. first item: streaming handshake microburst.
[03:58] Ravi: observed pattern — when microbursts hit and new sequence-length lanes are spawned, kernel selection acquires a global lock for compilation decisions. compile path is rare but expensive; concurrent compilations queue up and block the streaming handshake.
[04:15] Liam: can we avoid runtime compile by precompiling our common lanes? we have a stable model family for pilot.
[04:21] Ravi: yes, precompile is feasible — Redwood can bake compiled kernels into the model bundle for Dedicated or Private runs. on hosted we can pre-warm those lanes proactively.
[04:33] Jenna: any CI risk? if we precompile and then roll to a slightly different model checkpoint we might mismatch.
[04:40] Ravi: we version the compiled kernels tied to model hash; if checkpoint changes we fallback to the safe generic kernel while a background compile runs. the fallback can increase latency for some requests — that's the observed microburst.
[04:56] Sara: I want to understand the fallback policy — is it per-request or per-machine?
[05:00] Ravi: per-worker process. a process either has a compiled kernel for a lane or not. requests to that process hit the fallback until compile completes.
[05:10] Marco: what about hedging? could we send a duplicate request to another worker with precompiled lanes?
[05:16] Ravi: hedging helps but costs double tokens. for critical UX flows we used a 50ms hedging window and kept one probe to a cache-warmed worker; it reduced tail a lot in our internal tests.
[05:30] Jenna: but cost is a concern. Sara: we'd want to cap hedging to only top-level authentication/short responses, not long-batch jobs.
[05:45] Maya: next item from last week: seqlen bucketing — you tried dynamic re-bucketing. results?
[05:53] Ravi: yes. we adjusted batching boundaries to keep most requests in the short lane (<=32). batching efficiency improved ~18% and median latencies decreased, but we saw increase in 95th when traffic had sudden jumps in long sequences.
[06:09] Liam: does your batching introduce head-of-line blocking?
[06:12] Ravi: it can if a batch waits for a straggler, that's why we introduced a short timeout for short-lane batches (8ms) to flush quickly; longer lanes have slightly higher timeout to maximize throughput.
[06:24] Jenna: any suggestions for our tail — we saw 99th due to intermittent 512-seqlen jobs sneaking in and blocking GPUs.
[06:33] Ravi: two suggestions: strict request classification at ingress so large-seq requests get routed to isolated capacity; and a priority queue with small fast-path pool for short requests. Redwood Dedicated supports a reserved pool for short-lane traffic which prevents head-of-line.
[06:54] Sara: cost we need to model. Maya, can you provide numbers on cost delta for maintaining a reserved short-lane pool?
[07:00] Maya: yes, I'll include a couple of sizing scenarios in the spreadsheet — small, medium, and dedicated reserved pool with burst windows.
[07:08] Liam: another question — encryption in flight and audit logs. last week we asked about per-request metadata retention for debugging.
[07:16] Ravi: audit logs can be retained in your account region, and payloads can be masked. Redwood supports KMS integration for key management; for Private deployments you control the HSM.
[07:27] Marco: good. please send SOC2 and the redaction checklist.
[07:30] Maya: we'll attach the security pack after the call.
[07:36] Ravi: back to technical — kernel selection strategies: we ran three archetypes in bench: generic kernel, seqlen-specialized kernel, and quantized fast-warm kernel. tradeoffs: generic = robust but slower, seqlen-specialized = lowest median, quantized-fast = best warm-up.
[07:58] Jenna: which do you recommend for our pilot?
[08:00] Ravi: given your distribution (70% short), start with seqlen-specialized for short lane plus quantized-fast as a fallback for new workers; also enable proactive kernel precompile during off-peak.
[08:14] Jenna: about proactive precompile — what's the CPU/GPU overhead during precompile windows?
[08:19] Ravi: compile is CPU heavy; it can also take a GPU spool if kernels need autotuning. on Dedicated we can do precompile on separate compile instances to avoid impacting inference workers.
[08:33] Liam: that would be safest for us. we'll need a network diagram for the compile subnet.
[08:38] Maya: we'll coordinate a short design session.
[08:41] [00:09:00] — Sara joins: hey all, sorry for being late, was on another call.
[09:05] Sara: thanks for the summary. I want to be pragmatic — we don't need perfect 99.99th for pilot, just repeatable 95% under 100ms. let's map a small dedicated short-lane pool and run mixed traffic.
[09:20] Ravi: propose configuration: dedicated short-pool 2 workers (pinned), precompile top 3 lane kernels, quantized fallback enabled, hedging only for auth flow with 50ms probe. gives median ~30ms and 95th ~120-140ms in our sim.
[09:37] Jenna: those sims assume uniform worker health — what about failover? if a worker goes down do we see cascading compiles?
[09:45] Ravi: we saw cascades when many new workers spin up at once — mitigation: use warm standby instances and stagger scale-up with jitter. also can persist compiled kernels in a shared cache so new workers can fetch compiled artifacts instead of compiling.
[09:59] Marco: fetching compiled kernels still needs to respect your checksum / signing. acceptable if signed by Redwood and verifiable by our KMS.
[10:08] Ravi: yes we sign artifacts and we can publish signatures to your key.
[10:12] Lily: (small pause) — not in call? [laughter]
[10:16] Maya: okay final section — experiments and schedule. we propose two immediate tasks: 1) run a hedging-limited test on your staging with 10k traces and collect TTFT percentiles; 2) run seqlen bucket test (32 vs 64) with prefix cache toggled.
[10:33] Jenna: will run both. question on instrumentation — what format do you want the traces in?
[10:37] Ravi: send us CSV with timestamp, request id, seq_len, worker_id, kernel_variant, ttf_first_token_ms, ttf_stream_init_ms; we'll merge it into the perf workbook.
[10:49] Jenna: okay we'll export from our tracing.
[10:53] Maya: logistics — deliverables and dates?
[10:55] Ravi: Redwood will share kernel selection matrix and the compile artifact plan by 2026-07-01.
[10:59] Maya: and I'll send pricing scenarios and SLA notes by tomorrow 2026-06-30.
[11:03] Jenna: team will run tests and return traces by 2026-07-05.
[11:08] Sara: schedule the network/VPC peering discussion for the week of 2026-07-12 if needed.
[11:14] Maya: noted. any other questions?
[11:19] Marco: one last ask — if you can include a short doc describing the fallback to quantized kernel and any known quality regressions, that'll help us sign off.
[11:28] Ravi: will do, short note + signal metrics.
[11:31] Maya: perfect. thanks all. recap in chat, will follow up with attachments.
[11:36] Jenna: thanks, appreciate it. bye.

Summary: Mid-pilot check-in focused on TTFT and streaming microburst tail. Action plan: precompile common kernels, deploy small dedicated short-lane pool, enable quantized fallback, limited hedging for auth flows, and run staged traces. Pricing and security docs to be shared.

Questions noted: acceptable hedging budget, KMS signing for compiled artifacts, and seqlen bucketing thresholds.

References/links: perf_workbook_shared_link (sent in chat); security-pack.pdf (to be attached).

End of transcript.
